Urban II. Originally Odo of Châtillon, he reigned as pope from 1088 to 1099. A key administrative reformer, he continued the Gregorian Reforms. He is most famous for launching the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont, which mobilized Western European nobility to capture Jerusalem from Muslim rule.

In 1095, Urban preached the sermon at the Council of Clermont that launched the First Crusade. He called upon Western European Christians to reclaim the Holy Land with the famous rallying cry "Deus vult"—God wills it. He centralized the papal administration by establishing the Roman Curia, organizing the treasury and papal chancery into a highly efficient bureaucracy. He responded to Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who requested aid against the Seljuk Turks, aiming to restore relations and potentially reunite the Eastern and Western Churches.

Urban excommunicated King Philip I of France for unlawful marriage after the king repudiated his wife Bertha of Holland to marry Bertrade de Montfort. He died in July 1099, just two weeks after crusader forces captured Jerusalem, but before news of the victory could reach Rome. His pontificate established the papacy as a central political force capable of coordinating international military actions.
